Monism is a philosophical belief that says all of reality is, at its deepest level, one single thing — one substance, one principle, or one fundamental "stuff" that everything in the universe is made of or reduces down to.

Think of it this way. Look around you. You see a chair, a wall, your own body, your thoughts, the light coming through the window. These all look like completely different things. But a monist says: beneath all these surface differences, there is only one underlying reality. Everything you see, touch, think, or feel is just a different expression, form, or mode of that one thing.

The word itself, as a noun, refers to this doctrine or position as a whole. When someone says "monism," they mean the philosophical stance that the universe is unified at its most fundamental level.
The Problem Monism Is Trying to Answer

To really understand monism, you need to understand the question it's answering: What is the world ultimately made of?

Philosophers have long wrestled with the fact that reality seems to contain two very different kinds of things:

  • Physical things — rocks, trees, your brain, atoms, the stars
  • Mental things — your thoughts, feelings, consciousness, dreams, ideas

These two seem radically different. A rock has mass and takes up space. A thought doesn't. So how do they relate? Are they two completely separate things? Or is one of them secretly the other in disguise? Or are they both forms of something even more basic?

Monism's answer is bold and simple: there is only one fundamental kind of thing. Everything else is just that one thing wearing different clothes.

Monism is not one single view — it's a family of views. They all agree that reality is fundamentally one, but they disagree on what that one thing is.

1. Materialist Monism (also called Physicalism)

This is the most widely accepted form of monism in modern times, especially in science.

It says: everything is physical matter (or physical processes). Your thoughts, your emotions, your consciousness — all of it is just your brain doing physical things. There is no separate "mind stuff." Mind is what matter does when it's arranged in a very complex way, like a brain. This view says the universe is fundamentally one thing: the physical world.

Example: When you feel happy, a materialist monist says that happiness is just neurons firing in certain patterns in your brain. The feeling is the physical process — nothing more, nothing less.

2. Idealist Monism

This is the opposite. It says: everything is mind or consciousness. The physical world doesn't truly exist on its own — it only exists as experiences or ideas in a mind. What we call "matter" is ultimately mental.

The philosopher George Berkeley is famous for this view. He argued that to say a tree exists is simply to say that someone perceives it, or that God perceives it. There is no "tree out there" independent of any mind experiencing it.

Example: The chair you sit on isn't really a solid physical object existing on its own — it is a collection of sensory experiences (hardness, color, shape) existing within consciousness.

3. Neutral Monism

This version says: the one fundamental substance is neither mind nor matter — it is something neutral that gives rise to both. Mind and matter are just two sides of the same coin, two aspects of one deeper, more basic reality.

The philosopher Baruch Spinoza held a version of this. He said there is only one infinite substance — which he called God or Nature — and both mind and matter are just two of its infinitely many attributes or expressions.

Example: Think of a coin. On one side you see "heads," on the other "tails." But there is only one coin. Mind and matter are like heads and tails — different aspects of the same one underlying reality.

4. Priority Monism

A more modern version, associated with philosopher Jonathan Schaffer. It doesn't say there's only one thing in the universe (obviously there are many objects), but it says there is only one fundamental whole — the entire universe taken as a single, unified entity — and everything else (all the individual parts, objects, people) derives its existence from that whole. The whole comes first; the parts are secondary.

Example: Rather than building reality up from atoms → molecules → cells → organisms, priority monism says reality starts from the top: the universe as a whole is what's real, and all the smaller things inside it are just portions or aspects of that whole.
How Monism Differs from Its Rivals

Understanding monism becomes even clearer when you compare it to the alternatives:

Dualism says reality has two fundamental substances or kinds. The most famous version is René Descartes' view that mind and body are two completely separate, distinct things — one is non-physical (the soul/mind), the other is physical (the body). Monism directly rejects this "two-thing" picture.

Pluralism says reality is made of many fundamentally different things or substances that cannot be reduced to a single one. Monism rejects this too, insisting on an underlying unity.

So the spectrum looks like this:

  • Monism → One fundamental thing
  • Dualism → Two fundamental things
  • Pluralism → Many fundamental things
Monism Beyond Philosophy: In Religion and Spirituality

Monism is not only a philosophical idea — it also appears powerfully in religion and spirituality.

Many religious traditions hold a monistic worldview, meaning they see all of existence as ultimately one divine or spiritual reality.

Advaita Vedanta (a school of Hindu philosophy) is one of the most developed examples. It teaches that the individual self (Atman) and the ultimate reality of the universe (Brahman) are, at the deepest level, identical — they are one and the same. The sense of being a separate individual self is called "maya" (illusion). True enlightenment, in this view, is realizing that separation is an illusion and that everything is one.

Spinoza's God (mentioned above) also blurs the line between philosophy and religion — he said God and Nature are one and the same thing, making his monism a kind of pantheism (the view that God is everything and everything is God).

Some strands of Sufism in Islam, Zen Buddhism, and Taoism also carry monistic themes, emphasizing the ultimate oneness of all things.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

What monism claimsEverything in reality is fundamentally one single substance, principle, or whole
The question it answersWhat is the universe really made of at its deepest level?
Materialist monismThat one thing is physical matter
Idealist monismThat one thing is mind or consciousness
Neutral monismThat one thing is neither mind nor matter, but something more basic that gives rise to both
Priority monismThe whole universe is the one fundamental thing; all parts derive from it
Its oppositeDualism (two things) or Pluralism (many things)
How the Word Is Used in a Sentence

• "His philosophy was a form of monism — he believed that what we call 'mind' and what we call 'matter' are simply two faces of the same underlying reality."
  • "Monism stands in sharp contrast to Descartes' dualism, which insisted that body and soul are entirely separate substances."
  • "Advaita Vedanta is one of history's most sophisticated forms of monism, teaching that the individual self and the universal self are ultimately one."
  • "Modern neuroscience implicitly supports a kind of monism — it treats consciousness as a product of physical brain processes, not as something separate."

Monism is the philosophical conviction that beneath the dazzling variety and apparent complexity of the world, there is a single unified reality. It's the universe saying, in effect, "I am one." Whether that oneness is made of matter, mind, or something beyond both — that's where the different versions of monism part ways. But they all share the same foundational intuition: multiplicity is surface, unity is depth.
